Hottentot seabream populations along the South African coast exhibit life-history traits shaped by their temperate reef environment. This initial mass reflects the modest energetic reserves available for the lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. As these free-swimming larvae grow and eventually recruit to benthic habitats, their development is tuned to local thermal regimes. At a sustained water temperature of 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C], field studies have documented a maximum lifespan of approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], indicating that individuals can persist for over thirteen years under favorable conditions. This longevity is relatively extended for a sparid of moderate body size and is likely linked to the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy and the predictable productivity of the Benguela Current ecosystem.

Sexual maturation in the Hottentot seabream is a gradual process governed by both size and environmental cues. Individuals typically attain puberty at a standard length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of gametogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 194 grams [Wwp = approximately 194 grams], based on the species' length-weight relationship. This body mass at maturity is moderate compared to congeneric species, allowing individuals to allocate resources toward reproductive effort without having completed full somatic growth. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for such individuals is approximately 1,854 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,854 grams], representing the largest recorded body mass for the species based on empirical length-weight regressions.

Reproductive output in the Hottentot seabream is closely tied to the seasonal thermal cycle experienced across its temperate distribution. The index reflects a strategy of moderate, sustained reproductive allocation rather than a single, high-intensity spawning event. Gravid individuals collected during summer months typically show elevated GSI values that decline steadily as the spawning season progresses, with the thermal regime acting as the primary environmental cue for the initiation of vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation.

The early life history of the Hottentot seabream is characterized by a rapid transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition. Following chorion rupture, the prolarvae remain lecithotrophic for a brief period, absorbing yolk reserves before the mouth opens and first prey capture becomes possible. This trophic switch is a critical bottleneck in the species' recruitment dynamics, as variability in prey availability during the first-feeding stage can strongly influence year-class strength. The pelagic larval duration extends for several weeks before metamorphosis and settlement onto shallow reef habitats.

Comparative growth trajectories among related sparids highlight the Hottentot seabream's relatively slow rate of mass gain. The estimated wet weight at puberty of 194 grams [Wwp = 194 grams] is attained at a standard length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], a size that represents approximately half of the ultimate standard length of 46 centimeters [Li = 46 centimeters].
